paper.title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

scenes.title: Bigger indexes buried good pages under junk
scenes.narration: By 1997, search engines indexed tens of millions of pages, but people still only read the first few results. Search 'bill clinton' and the pages you want drown in grey junk; most engines couldn't even find their own homepage.
scenes.quote: "Junk results" often wash out any results that a user is interested in. In fact, as of November 1997, only one of the top four commercial search engines finds itself

diagram.title: Bigger indexes buried good pages under junk
diagram.caption: By November 1997 top engines claimed up to 100 million pages, but people still read only the first few tens of results. Junk results wash out the pages users want, and only one of the top four engines could find itself (pp. 2–3).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the index size slider and watch whitehouse.gov sink below the line where people stop reading.
diagram.html: 100M

explorables.label: Index size explosion
explorables.blurb: Search indexes grew from about 110,000 pages in 1994 to as many as 100 million by late 1997, with over a billion foreseen by 2000. More pages meant many more weak matches for any query.
explorables.quote: In 1994, one of the first web search engines, the World Wide Web Worm (WWWW) [McBryan 94] had an index of 110,000 web pages and web accessible documents.

explorables.label: People stop reading
explorables.blurb: Indexes grew by orders of magnitude, but readers did not look at more results. A good page ranked below the first screenful is effectively never seen.
explorables.quote: the number of documents in the indices has been increasing by many orders of magnitude, but the user’s ability to look at documents has not. People are still only willing to look at the first few tens of results.

explorables.label: Junk results
explorables.blurb: A complete index is not enough: low-quality pages that happen to match the query words crowd out the pages a user actually wants. The paper cites a real engine returning a 'Bill Clinton Sucks' page.
explorables.quote: the completeness of the index is not the only factor in the quality of search results. "Junk results" often wash out any results that a user is interested in.

explorables.label: Can't find itself
explorables.blurb: A telling test: search for an engine's own name. In November 1997, only one of the four leading commercial engines put its own search page in its top ten.
explorables.quote: as of November 1997, only one of the top four commercial search engines finds itself (returns its own search page in response to its name in the top ten results).

explorables.label: Precision over recall
explorables.blurb: Because people only read the top of the list, the goal becomes getting the very best pages into the top results, even if some relevant pages are never returned.
explorables.quote: as the collection size grows, we need tools that have very high precision (number of relevant documents returned, say in the top tens of results).

scenes.explanation: By 1998 the web had grown to tens of millions of pages, and older search engines returned lots of 'junk' — pages barely related to the query — because there was no good way to separate high-quality pages from spam. Bigger indexes did not mean better answers: they could bury the page users actually wanted, like whitehouse.gov, under grey noise, and some engines could not even find their own homepage. This is the problem the paper opens with. It motivates looking beyond keyword matching toward a quality signal drawn from the web's own structure, which later scenes introduce.

scenes.title: Word matching rewards short, low-quality pages
scenes.narration: Classic information retrieval scores a page by how closely its words match the query. On the uncontrolled web, that crowns tiny pages that are little more than the query words, and anyone can game it.
scenes.quote: For example, we have seen a major search engine return a page containing only "Bill Clinton Sucks" and picture from a "Bill Clinton" query.

diagram.title: Word matching rewards short, low-quality pages
diagram.caption: The standard vector space model scores a page by how closely its word occurrences match the query, so on the web it favors tiny pages that are the query plus a few words, and hidden text can game it (p. 6).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the White House page shorter until it wins, then switch off the hidden text on the spam page.

explorables.label: Vector space score
explorables.blurb: Classic IR turns the query and each page into word-count vectors and returns the page whose vector is closest to the query's. The cosine numbers here are illustrative, but they show how length dilutes the match.
explorables.quote: the standard vector space model tries to return the document that most closely approximates the query, given that both query and document are vectors defined by their word occurrence.

explorables.label: The tiny junk page
explorables.blurb: A page that is little more than the query words is the closest possible match, so word matching puts it on top. The paper saw a major engine return exactly such a page for 'Bill Clinton'.
explorables.quote: On the web, this strategy often returns very short documents that are the query plus a few words.

explorables.label: Hidden-text gaming
explorables.blurb: Because anyone can publish anything, spammers stuff invisible query words into pages to win word-match rankings. The paper notes this is why metadata efforts largely failed.
explorables.quote: metadata efforts have largely failed with web search engines, because any text on the page which is not directly represented to the user is abused to manipulate search engines.

explorables.label: Tidy vs. wild data
explorables.blurb: IR methods were benchmarked on small, controlled collections like TREC, far smaller and cleaner than the web. Techniques that shine there often break on the web.
explorables.quote: benchmark is only 20GB compared to the 147GB from our crawl of 24 million web pages. Things that work well on TREC often do not produce good results on the web.

scenes.explanation: Classic information retrieval ranks a document by how closely its words match the query, a method built for small, curated collections like libraries. On the open web anyone can publish anything, so this approach rewards tiny, manipulated pages — famously, a major search engine once returned a page containing only 'Bill Clinton Sucks' and a picture for a 'Bill Clinton' query. This showed word frequency alone could not measure quality or trustworthiness, and that the uncontrolled, gameable nature of web data breaks assumptions built into traditional IR. It sets up the case for a harder-to-fake signal: links from other pages.
scenes.section: 3.2 Differences Between the Web and Well Controlled Collections

scenes.title: Links are votes, and link text describes the target
scenes.narration: Google's insight: use the web's hypertext. Orange arrows pointing at whitehouse.gov act as citations that signal quality, and the words on those links, the anchor text, get attached to the page they point to.
scenes.quote: In particular, link structure [Page 98] and link text provide a lot of information for making relevance judgments and quality filtering.

diagram.title: Links are votes, and link text describes the target
diagram.caption: Google treats hyperlinks as citations that signal quality. It also attaches each link's anchor text to the page the link points to, which even lets it return uncrawled pages like whitehouse.gov (pp. 3–5, 13).
diagram.tryHint: Try: switch where link text belongs, then slide the number of linking pages down to zero.
diagram.html:
Link text belongs to:
Next: should a link from Yahoo! count the same as one from an obscure page?

explorables.label: Anchor text
explorables.blurb: The clickable words of a link. Google indexes them as words of the page the link points to, not only the page the link sits on.
explorables.quote: Most search engines associate the text of a link with the page that the link is on. In addition, we associate it with the page the link points to.

explorables.label: Uncrawled whitehouse.gov
explorables.blurb: In Google's real 'bill clinton' results, the top whitehouse.gov hit had no title because it was never crawled. Anchor text alone showed it was a good answer.
explorables.quote: Notice that there is no title for the first result. This is because it was not crawled. Instead, Google relied on anchor text to determine this was a good answer to the query.

explorables.label: Links as votes
explorables.blurb: Borrowed from academic citation analysis: every link pointing to a page is a citation hinting that the page is worth reading. Here, the red bar simply counts incoming links.
explorables.quote: Academic citation literature has been applied to the web, largely by counting citations or backlinks to a given page. This gives some approximation of a page’s importance or quality.

explorables.label: Word-match junk page
explorables.blurb: A tiny page that is little more than the query words matches perfectly on text, but nobody links to it. Link signals push it below well-cited pages.
explorables.quote: we have seen a major search engine return a page containing only "Bill Clinton Sucks" and picture from a "Bill Clinton" query.

scenes.explanation: Google's core idea reframes a hyperlink as a citation: a page linking to whitehouse.gov is effectively casting a vote that whitehouse.gov is worth visiting, and pages with more such votes deserve more trust. Just as important, the clickable text of the link, the anchor text, gets attributed to the page it points to, so a page can be found and described using words that never appear on it. This lets Google index pages, even ones it hasn't crawled, purely from what others say about them. It bridges the word-matching problem of the last scene to the PageRank formula in the next.
scenes.section: 2.1 PageRank: Bringing Order to the Web · 2.2 Anchor Text

scenes.title: A page is important if important pages link to it
scenes.narration: PageRank gives each page a base share (1−d), then adds rank flowing in from every linking page, split evenly across that page's outgoing links. With d = 0.85, it's the chance a random surfer lands there.
scenes.quote: PageRank extends this idea by not counting links from all pages equally, and by normalizing by the number of links on a page. PageRank is defined as follows:

diagram.title: A page is important if important pages link to it
diagram.caption: PageRank counts each incoming link as the linker's own rank divided by its number of outgoing links, scaled by d (usually 0.85), plus a base share (1−d) (p. 4).
diagram.tryHint: Try: raise C(T1) to split T1's vote across more links and watch whitehouse.gov's red bar shrink.
diagram.html:
PR(A)=(1−d)+d(PR(T1)C(T1)+…+PR(Tn)C(Tn))
PR(A) — whitehouse.gov's rank, the thing we compute
(1−d) — a base share every page gets, links or not
d — weight given to incoming links; usually 0.85
PR(T1)/C(T1) — a linker's rank, split evenly over its C outgoing links
+ … + — add a share from every linking page; their ranks come from the same formula

Toy PR and C values are illustrative; grey dots are the linker's other outgoing links. The paper computes PageRank for 26 million pages in a few hours (p. 4) — next: the pipeline that gathers those links.

explorables.label: Base share (1−d)
explorables.blurb: Every page starts with (1−d) no matter who links to it. In the random-surfer story, this is the surfer getting bored and jumping to a random page.
explorables.quote: And, the d damping factor is the probability at each page the "random surfer" will get bored and request another random page.

explorables.label: Damping factor d
explorables.blurb: d sets how much of a page's rank comes from incoming links versus the flat base share. The authors usually set it to 0.85.
explorables.quote: The parameter d is a damping factor which can be set between 0 and 1. We usually set d to 0.85.

explorables.label: Normalized vote PR/C
explorables.blurb: A link is not a flat vote: it carries the linking page's own rank, divided by how many links that page has. A page with many outgoing links gives each one a smaller share.
explorables.quote: PageRank extends this idea by not counting links from all pages equally, and by normalizing by the number of links on a page.

explorables.label: Recursive propagation
explorables.blurb: Each linker's rank is itself computed with the same formula, so weight flows through the whole link graph. Many modest links or one link from a high-rank page can both lift a page.
explorables.quote: a page can have a high PageRank if there are many pages that point to it, or if there are some pages that point to it and have a high PageRank.

explorables.label: Random surfer
explorables.blurb: PageRank can be read as the chance that a surfer who clicks links at random, occasionally jumping to a random page, ends up on whitehouse.gov.
explorables.quote: never hitting "back" but eventually gets bored and starts on another random page. The probability that the random surfer visits a page is its PageRank.

scenes.explanation: PageRank formalizes 'links as votes' into a formula: every page starts with a base share of importance, (1−d), then gains additional rank flowing in from every page that links to it. Each linking page T splits its own rank PR(T) evenly across all C(T) of its outgoing links, so a link from a selective page carries more weight than one from a page linking to everything. The damping factor d, set to 0.85, is the probability a 'random surfer' clicking links keeps going rather than jumping elsewhere, and because rank depends on other pages' rank, the calculation repeats recursively until it settles.

scenes.title: From crawl to answer: Google's full pipeline
scenes.narration: Crawlers fetch pages into a compressed repository. The indexer turns words into hits in barrels and extracts anchors, links feed PageRank, and the sorter inverts barrels by word, so the searcher can answer 'bill clinton'.
scenes.quote: Figure 1. High Level Google Architecture

diagram.title: From crawl to answer: Google's full pipeline
diagram.caption: Redrawn from Fig. 1 (p. 7). The stages follow Section 4.1 (p. 7): crawl, index, resolve links, sort, search. Sizes come from Table 1 (p. 14) and the sample result from Fig. 4 (p. 13).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the stage slider to watch each part of the pipeline light up and pass data along its arrows.
diagram.html: 5 · Search

explorables.label: Repository
explorables.blurb: The Repository holds the full compressed HTML of every crawled page, each prefixed by its docID, length and URL. Every other data structure can be rebuilt from it.
explorables.quote: The storeserver then compresses and stores the web pages into a repository. Every web page has an associated ID number called a docID which is assigned whenever a new URL is parsed out of a web page.

explorables.label: Indexer and hits
explorables.blurb: The Indexer parses each page into hits: word occurrences with position, font size and capitalization. It spreads the hits across barrels as a partially sorted forward index.
explorables.quote: Each document is converted into a set of word occurrences called hits. The hits record the word, position in document, an approximation of font size, and capitalization.

explorables.label: URL Resolver
explorables.blurb: The URL Resolver reads the Anchors file and turns link URLs into docIDs. It credits each anchor text to the page the link points to, and outputs the links database that PageRank runs on.
explorables.quote: It puts the anchor text into the forward index, associated with the docID that the anchor points to. It also generates a database of links which are pairs of docIDs.

explorables.label: Sorter / inverted index
explorables.blurb: The Sorter re-sorts each barrel from docID order into wordID order. This gives the searcher, for any word, a list of the documents containing it.
explorables.quote: The sorter takes the barrels, which are sorted by docID (this is a simplification, see Section 4.2.5), and resorts them by wordID to generate the inverted index.

explorables.label: Searcher
explorables.blurb: The Searcher answers a query like 'bill clinton' by combining the lexicon, the inverted index and the PageRanks. It then ranks the matching documents.
explorables.quote: The searcher is run by a web server and uses the lexicon built by DumpLexicon together with the inverted index and the PageRanks to answer queries.

scenes.explanation: This diagram traces a query through Google's whole pipeline in the order data actually flows. Crawlers download raw pages into a compressed Repository; the Indexer reads it, turns words into 'hits' sorted into Barrels, and separately extracts every link's anchor text and destination, feeding the link graph used for PageRank via the URL Resolver. The Sorter then rebuilds those barrels into an inverted index organized by word rather than by document, and the Searcher uses that index plus PageRank to answer a live query like 'bill clinton.' Each earlier idea, the junk problem, links as votes, and the PageRank math, becomes one stage here.

scenes.title: Ranking blends hit types, proximity and PageRank
scenes.narration: For each matching page, green hits are counted by type (title, anchor, big font) and by how close 'bill' sits to 'clinton'. Those weighted counts form an IR score, then the red PageRank bar is mixed in.
scenes.quote: We take the dot product of the vector of count-weights with the vector of type-weights to compute an IR score for the document. Finally, the IR score is combined with PageRank to give a final rank to the document.

diagram.title: Ranking blends hit types, proximity and PageRank
diagram.caption: For each matching page, Google counts hits by type and proximity and tapers the counts. It dots them with weights to get an IR score, then combines that score with PageRank for the final rank (p. 12).
diagram.tryHint: Try: switch to the junk page and drag small-font repeats up to 30. The tapered count barely moves its rank.

explorables.label: Hit types
explorables.blurb: Each occurrence of a query word is tagged by where it appears, such as in the title, in anchor text, in the URL, or in large or small plain text. Each type gets its own weight.
explorables.quote: Google considers each hit to be one of several different types (title, anchor, URL, plain text large font, plain text small font, ...), each of which has its own type-weight.

explorables.label: Tapered count-weights
explorables.blurb: Raw hit counts are converted into count-weights that grow at first and then flatten out. Repeating a word many times stops helping, which blunts keyword stuffing.
explorables.quote: Count-weights increase linearly with counts at first but quickly taper off so that more than a certain count will not help.

explorables.label: Proximity bins
explorables.blurb: For multi-word queries, matched hits are grouped by how far apart they sit. The distance falls into one of 10 bins, from a phrase match to 'not even close'. Each type and proximity pair has its own weight.
explorables.quote: The proximity is based on how far apart the hits are in the document (or anchor) but is classified into 10 different value "bins" ranging from a phrase match to "not even close".

explorables.label: IR score
explorables.blurb: The IR score is the dot product of the count-weight vector with the type-weight vector. For multi-word queries, it uses the type-prox-weights instead. It measures how well the page's text matches the query.
explorables.quote: We take the dot product of the vector of count-weights with the vector of type-weights to compute an IR score for the document.

explorables.label: Mixing in PageRank
explorables.blurb: The text-based IR score is combined with the page's PageRank to produce its final rank. The ranking function is designed so that no single factor dominates. The paper does not give the exact formula.
explorables.quote: Finally, the IR score is combined with PageRank to give a final rank to the document.

scenes.explanation: For a candidate page, Google doesn't just check that 'bill' and 'clinton' appear, it notes where they appear, such as title, anchor text, or large font, and how close together they sit, since prominent, nearby matches suggest a better result. These counts, weighted by hit type and proximity, are combined via a dot product into a single IR (information retrieval) score. That score is then mixed with the page's PageRank to produce the final rank, so a page can win by strong textual match, by broad importance, or a mix of both. This is where anchor text from scene 3 and PageRank from scene 4 both feed one ranking decision.

scenes.title: 24 million pages indexed in under a week
scenes.narration: The prototype crawled 24 million pages, compressing 147.8 GB into a 53.5 GB repository, with a 55.2 GB index. 'bill clinton' returned whitehouse.gov pages, some found via anchor text alone, with no broken links.
scenes.quote: the crawling, indexing, and sorting operations are efficient enough to be able to build an index of a substantial portion of the web -- 24 million pages, in less than one week.

diagram.title: 24 million pages indexed in under a week
diagram.caption: The prototype fetched 24 million pages (147.8 GB), zlib-compressed them into a 53.5 GB repository, and needed about 55.2 GB for everything else (p. 14). All of this was built in under a week (p. 16). For 'bill clinton' it returned whitehouse.gov pages, some found only through anchor text, and none were broken links (p. 13).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the pages-crawled slider toward 100 M to see how storage and build time would grow if every stage scales linearly.

explorables.label: 24 M pages in a week
explorables.blurb: Crawling, indexing and sorting together built an index of 24 million pages in under a week. The authors expected 100 million pages to take less than a month, because every time-consuming stage runs in parallel and in roughly linear time.
explorables.quote: the crawling, indexing, and sorting operations are efficient enough to be able to build an index of a substantial portion of the web -- 24 million pages, in less than one week.

explorables.label: 53.5 GB repository
explorables.blurb: Every page's full HTML is kept, compressed with zlib at about 3 to 1. That shrinks 147.8 GB of fetched pages to 53.5 GB, which makes the raw web a cheap resource for research.
explorables.quote: Due to compression the total size of the repository is about 53 GB, just over one third of the total data it stores.

explorables.label: 55.2 GB for the rest
explorables.blurb: Everything else the engine uses totals about 55 GB: inverted indexes, the lexicon, the document index and the links database. Most queries need only the 4.1 GB short inverted index.
explorables.quote: More importantly, the total of all the data used by the search engine requires a comparable amount of storage, about 55 GB.

explorables.label: Found via anchor text
explorables.blurb: The top whitehouse.gov result has no title because it was never crawled. Google ranked it using only the text of links pointing to it. The mailto result was found the same way.
explorables.quote: Notice that there is no title for the first result. This is because it was not crawled. Instead, Google relied on anchor text to determine this was a good answer to the query.

explorables.label: No broken links
explorables.blurb: The red bars are PageRank percentages. The authors credit high PageRank for keeping every returned result a reasonably high quality, working page.
explorables.quote: All of the results are reasonably high quality pages and, at last check, none were broken links. This is largely because they all have high PageRank.

scenes.explanation: Brin and Page validated their design on a real prototype: crawling and indexing 24 million pages in under a week, compressing 147.8 GB of raw HTML into a 53.5 GB repository, with roughly 55.2 GB used by the rest of the index. Searching 'bill clinton' surfaced whitehouse.gov pages, including some found only through anchor text pointing to them rather than their own content, and the results contained no broken links. This scene shows the ideas from earlier scenes, PageRank, anchor text, and the pipeline, actually worked at web scale, not just in theory.

scenes.title: Quality was judged by eye, and queries took seconds
scenes.narration: The quality claims rest on the authors' own experience, not a user study. Queries took 1 to 10 seconds without caching, and scaling far past 100 million pages was an open challenge.
scenes.quote: Of course a true test of the quality of a search engine would involve an extensive user study or results analysis which we do not have room for here.

diagram.title: Quality was judged by eye, and queries took seconds
diagram.caption: The authors judged result quality from their own experience, not a user study (p. 13). Queries took 1 to 10 seconds, mostly waiting on disk IO (pp. 14–15). Growing much past 100 million pages was left as an open problem (p. 19).
diagram.tryHint: Try: switch between Initial and Repeated queries, then slide the index size past 100M.
diagram.html:
Quality was judged by eye, and queries took seconds

Run:
24M

explorables.label: Judged by eye
explorables.blurb: The claim that Google beat commercial engines rests on the authors' own experience with searches like "bill clinton", not on measured relevance scores.
explorables.quote: While a complete user evaluation is beyond the scope of this paper, our own experience with Google has shown it to produce better results than the major commercial search engines for most searches.

explorables.label: The missing user study
explorables.blurb: The authors say a real quality test would need a large user study or results analysis. They leave it out and invite readers to try the engine themselves.
explorables.quote: Of course a true test of the quality of a search engine would involve an extensive user study or results analysis which we do not have room for here.

explorables.label: Waiting on disk IO
explorables.blurb: Most query time went to reading data from disks spread across machines over NFS, not to CPU work. When the same query was repeated with IO mostly cached, it got much faster.
explorables.quote: The current version of Google answers most queries in between 1 and 10 seconds. This time is mostly dominated by disk IO over NFS (since disks are spread over a number of machines).

explorables.label: Beyond 100M pages
explorables.blurb: At about 100 million pages the system would run into operating system limits such as addressable memory, file descriptors and sockets. Going much further was left as an open problem.
explorables.quote: We believe expanding to a lot more than 100 million pages would greatly increase the complexity of our system.

scenes.explanation: The paper is candid about its own limits: the authors judged search quality from their own experience using the system rather than a formal, blinded user study, since they didn't have room to run one. Query response time was 1 to 10 seconds without caching, dominated by disk I/O rather than computation, which would need to improve for production use. The authors also flag that scaling far beyond the 24-million-page prototype toward hundreds of millions of pages was an open engineering challenge they had not yet solved. This tempers the strong results in the previous scene with a clear list of what remained unproven.

walkthrough.citation: Brin, S., & Page, L. (1998). The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine. Computer Networks and ISDN Systems, 30(1–7), 107–117.

takeaways.idea: Links act as votes; pages linked by important pages become important.
takeaways.tryIt: Raise C(T1) to split T1's vote across more links and watch whitehouse.gov's PageRank bar shrink.

takeaways.idea: Anchor text lets a page be found by words it never contains.
takeaways.tryIt: Switch where the link text belongs, then slide linking pages down to zero to see anchor text vanish.

takeaways.idea: Google's pipeline separates crawling, indexing, sorting, and ranking into stages.
takeaways.tryIt: Drag the stage slider to watch data flow from Repository through Barrels to the Searcher.

takeaways.idea: 24 million pages were crawled and indexed in under a week.
takeaways.tryIt: Drag the pages-crawled slider toward 100M to see how storage would grow if scaling stayed linear.

takeaways.idea: Search quality was judged by eye, not a formal user study.
takeaways.tryIt: Switch between Initial and Repeated queries, then push index size past 100M to see the open scaling question.

scenes.narration: PageRank gives each page a base share (1−d), then adds rank flowing in from every linking page, split evenly across that page's outgoing links. With d = 0.85, it's the chance a random surfer lands there.
scenes.quote: PageRank extends this idea by not counting links from all pages equally, and by normalizing by the number of links on a page. PageRank is defined as follows:
scenes.explanation: PageRank formalizes 'links as votes' into a formula: every page starts with a base share of importance, (1−d), then gains additional rank flowing in from every page that links to it. Each linking page T splits its own rank PR(T) evenly across all C(T) of its outgoing links, so a link from a selective page carries more weight than one from a page linking to everything. The damping factor d, set to 0.85, is the probability a 'random surfer' clicking links keeps going rather than jumping elsewhere, and because rank depends on other pages' rank, the calculation repeats recursively until it settles.

scenes.title: From crawl to answer: Google's full pipeline
scenes.narration: Crawlers fetch pages into a compressed repository. The indexer turns words into hits in barrels and extracts anchors, links feed PageRank, and the sorter inverts barrels by word, so the searcher can answer 'bill clinton'.
scenes.quote: Figure 1. High Level Google Architecture
scenes.explanation: This diagram traces a query through Google's whole pipeline in the order data actually flows. Crawlers download raw pages into a compressed Repository; the Indexer reads it, turns words into 'hits' sorted into Barrels, and separately extracts every link's anchor text and destination, feeding the link graph used for PageRank via the URL Resolver. The Sorter then rebuilds those barrels into an inverted index organized by word rather than by document, and the Searcher uses that index plus PageRank to answer a live query like 'bill clinton.' Each earlier idea, the junk problem, links as votes, and the PageRank math, becomes one stage here.

scenes.title: Ranking blends hit types, proximity and PageRank
scenes.narration: For each matching page, green hits are counted by type (title, anchor, big font) and by how close 'bill' sits to 'clinton'. Those weighted counts form an IR score, then the red PageRank bar is mixed in.
scenes.quote: We take the dot product of the vector of count-weights with the vector of type-weights to compute an IR score for the document. Finally, the IR score is combined with PageRank to give a final rank to the document.
scenes.explanation: For a candidate page, Google doesn't just check that 'bill' and 'clinton' appear, it notes where they appear, such as title, anchor text, or large font, and how close together they sit, since prominent, nearby matches suggest a better result. These counts, weighted by hit type and proximity, are combined via a dot product into a single IR (information retrieval) score. That score is then mixed with the page's PageRank to produce the final rank, so a page can win by strong textual match, by broad importance, or a mix of both. This is where anchor text from scene 3 and PageRank from scene 4 both feed one ranking decision.

scenes.title: 24 million pages indexed in under a week
scenes.narration: The prototype crawled 24 million pages, compressing 147.8 GB into a 53.5 GB repository, with a 55.2 GB index. 'bill clinton' returned whitehouse.gov pages, some found via anchor text alone, with no broken links.
scenes.quote: the crawling, indexing, and sorting operations are efficient enough to be able to build an index of a substantial portion of the web -- 24 million pages, in less than one week.
scenes.explanation: Brin and Page validated their design on a real prototype: crawling and indexing 24 million pages in under a week, compressing 147.8 GB of raw HTML into a 53.5 GB repository, with roughly 55.2 GB used by the rest of the index. Searching 'bill clinton' surfaced whitehouse.gov pages, including some found only through anchor text pointing to them rather than their own content, and the results contained no broken links. This scene shows the ideas from earlier scenes, PageRank, anchor text, and the pipeline, actually worked at web scale, not just in theory.

scenes.title: Quality was judged by eye, and queries took seconds
scenes.narration: The quality claims rest on the authors' own experience, not a user study. Queries took 1 to 10 seconds without caching, and scaling far past 100 million pages was an open challenge.
scenes.quote: Of course a true test of the quality of a search engine would involve an extensive user study or results analysis which we do not have room for here.
scenes.explanation: The paper is candid about its own limits: the authors judged search quality from their own experience using the system rather than a formal, blinded user study, since they didn't have room to run one. Query response time was 1 to 10 seconds without caching, dominated by disk I/O rather than computation, which would need to improve for production use. The authors also flag that scaling far beyond the 24-million-page prototype toward hundreds of millions of pages was an open engineering challenge they had not yet solved. This tempers the strong results in the previous scene with a clear list of what remained unproven.

papers.title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

scenes.title: RNNs must read one word at a time
scenes.narration: To understand "its", a recurrent network walks the sentence word by word, each step waiting on the last. That chain can't be split across the GPU, so training long sentences is slow.
scenes.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

diagram.title: RNNs must read one word at a time
diagram.caption: A recurrent network computes each hidden state from the previous one plus the current word, so this 13-token sentence takes 13 steps in strict order (p. 2). Table 1 lists O(n) sequential operations for recurrent layers (p. 6).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the time step slider, then press “Try computing all words at once” to see which steps are blocked.
diagram.html: RNNs must read one word at a time

explorables.label: Hidden state hₜ
explorables.blurb: Each circle is the RNN's memory after reading one more word. It is computed from the previous circle plus the current word, so it cannot exist before its predecessor.
explorables.quote: Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states ht, as a function of the previous hidden state ht−1 and the input for position t.

explorables.label: The sequential chain
explorables.blurb: The orange arrows are dependencies: step t must finish before step t+1 can begin. Within a single sentence the work cannot be split across GPU cores, and longer sentences make this worse.
explorables.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

explorables.label: O(n) sequential steps
explorables.blurb: For n words a recurrent layer needs n steps run one after another. The paper's Table 1 contrasts this with O(1) for self-attention.
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

explorables.label: Law → its path length
explorables.blurb: To link “its” back to “Law”, information has to pass through every hidden state in between. The paper argues that longer paths like this make long-range dependencies harder to learn.
explorables.quote: One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network.

explorables.label: Why “its”?
explorables.blurb: “its” refers back to “Law”, which is a classic anaphora. The paper's own attention plots show heads that link these two words directly.
explorables.quote: Two attention heads, also in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution.

scenes.title: Convolutions parallelize but distant words stay far apart
scenes.narration: Convolutional models like ByteNet and ConvS2S process all words at once. But linking "its" back to "Law" still takes several stacked layers, and the gap grows with distance, which makes long-range links harder to learn.
scenes.quote: In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet.

diagram.title: Convolutions parallelize but distant words stay far apart
diagram.caption: Convolutional models such as ByteNet and ConvS2S compute every position in parallel. Relating two positions still takes more operations as they get farther apart: linearly for ConvS2S, logarithmically for ByteNet (p. 2; Table 1, p. 6; p. 7).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the target-word slider away from “its”, then switch between contiguous and dilated kernels and watch the red path and layer count change.
diagram.html:
Layers needed to connect “its” ↔ “Law” (distance 7):
Contiguous (ConvS2S-style)
Dilated (ByteNet-style)
Self-attention (next scene)
1
Maximum path length between two positions (Table 1, p. 6; p. 7)
RecurrentO(n)
Convolutional, contiguous kernelsO(n/k)
Convolutional, dilated kernelsO(logk(n))
Self-attentionO(1)

Illustrative toy setup: kernel width 3, with dilation doubling each layer (1, 2, 4, 8). Green marks positions computed in parallel, red marks the path cost, and the dashed violet arc marks a direct attention link. Click any word tile to make it the target.

explorables.label: Why stack layers?
explorables.blurb: A kernel only covers a small window of neighbouring words. To connect two distant words, the signal has to pass up through several layers stacked on top of each other.
explorables.quote: A single convolutional layer with kernel width k < n does not connect all pairs of input and output positions.

explorables.label: Contiguous vs dilated
explorables.blurb: The shaded cone is what the top node for “its” can see. Contiguous kernels widen it by a fixed amount per layer, so reach grows linearly (O(n/k) layers). Dilated kernels skip positions, so reach grows exponentially and you need only O(log_k(n)) layers.
explorables.quote: Doing so requires a stack of O(n/k) convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or O(logk(n)) in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network.

explorables.label: Path length
explorables.blurb: The red path is the route a signal takes between the two words. The paper argues that longer paths make long-range dependencies harder to learn.
explorables.quote: The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies

explorables.label: Table 1 path lengths
explorables.blurb: Table 1 compares layer types by the maximum path length between two positions. Recurrent layers need O(n), convolutions need O(log_k(n)) with dilation, and self-attention needs O(1).
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

scenes.title: Let every word look directly at every other word
scenes.narration: The Transformer drops recurrence and convolution entirely. With self-attention, "its" connects to "Law" in a single step. Every pair of words is one hop apart, and all the arcs are computed in parallel.
scenes.quote: In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output.

diagram.title: Let every word look directly at every other word
diagram.caption: The Transformer relies entirely on attention instead of recurrence or convolution (p. 2). A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations, while a recurrent layer needs O(n) (p. 6).
diagram.tryHint: Try: click “application” or “The” to make it the query, then hover a far-away word to see that it is still one hop.
diagram.html:
Path length: 1 hop · O(1)Sequential ops: O(1) · all links at onceCost: 13 × 13 = 169 pair scores · O(n²·d)
Click a word to make it the query · arc thickness = illustrative weights

explorables.label: Self-attention
explorables.blurb: Each violet arc is a direct link from the query word to another word in the same sentence. The layer builds each word's new representation by mixing in information from all the others according to these link strengths.
explorables.quote: Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence.

explorables.label: One-hop path length
explorables.blurb: Any two words are joined by a single attention step, however far apart they are. A recurrent layer needs a chain of O(n) steps, and shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn.
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

explorables.label: Computed in parallel
explorables.blurb: No link has to wait for an earlier one, so all words are processed at once instead of one step at a time. This is why the base model reached state-of-the-art translation after about 12 hours on 8 GPUs.
explorables.quote: The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.

explorables.label: The n² cost
explorables.blurb: Linking every pair means n × n scores, giving O(n²·d) work per layer. This is cheaper than recurrence when the sentence length n is below the model dimension d. For very long inputs, the authors suggest restricting attention to a local neighborhood.
explorables.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position.

scenes.title: Attention is a soft lookup: query, keys, values
scenes.narration: "its" sends out a query and every word offers a key and a value. The model takes query-key dot products, divides them by the square root of the key size, and applies a softmax. The resulting weights blend the values.
scenes.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

diagram.title: Attention is a soft lookup: query, keys, values
diagram.caption: Scaled dot-product attention compares the query “its” with every key, divides each dot product by √dk, and applies a softmax. The resulting weights average the values (pp. 3–4). Each head uses dk = 64, and without the scaling, large dot products saturate the softmax (p. 4).
diagram.tryHint: Try: untick “Scale by 1/√dk” and drag the key size up to 512 to watch the softmax collapse onto one word.
diagram.html: Scores are illustrative (unit-scale q·k per word). Unscaled q·k is modeled as growing like √dk because its variance is dk (p. 4). The paper uses dk = 64 per head.

explorables.label: The query
explorables.blurb: The word doing the looking, here “its”, is turned into a query vector. That vector is compared against every word's key to decide where to look.
explorables.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

explorables.label: Keys and dot products
explorables.blurb: Each word offers a key, and a query–key dot product measures how well the two match. All the dot products for a sentence come out of a single matrix multiplication, which is why this method is fast.
explorables.quote: dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

explorables.label: Dividing by √dk
explorables.blurb: When the components have unit variance, a dot product over dk dimensions has variance dk, so raw scores grow with the key size. Dividing by √dk keeps the scores in a range where the softmax still has useful gradients.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

explorables.label: Softmax weights
explorables.blurb: The softmax turns the scaled scores into positive weights that sum to 1. The lookup is soft: every word gets some share, and the best matches get most of it.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

explorables.label: Weighted sum of values
explorables.blurb: The output for “its” is a weighted average of all the value vectors. In this illustration, most of the mix comes from “Law” and “application”.
explorables.quote: The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

scenes.title: Sine waves stamp word order onto the tiles
scenes.narration: Attention alone ignores word order, so each tile gets a sinusoidal position signal added to its embedding. These tiles flow through six encoder layers and six decoder layers, and masking stops the decoder from peeking at future words.
scenes.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

diagram.title: Sine waves stamp word order onto the tiles
diagram.caption: The Transformer has no recurrence or convolution, so a sinusoidal position signal is added to each word embedding (p. 6). The tiles then pass through 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, and masking keeps the decoder from seeing later words (p. 3, 5).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the position slider and watch each sine wave give that position its own pattern of values.
diagram.html: pos 8 → “its”

explorables.label: Sine waves per dimension
explorables.blurb: Each dimension of the position signal is a sine or cosine wave, and each pair of dimensions uses a slower frequency than the one before. Taken together, the values at a given position form a pattern that no other position shares.
explorables.quote: where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π.

explorables.label: Added, not appended
explorables.blurb: The position signal has the same size as the word embedding (512 in the paper), so the two are added together. Each tile then carries both what the word is and where it sits.
explorables.quote: To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension dmodel as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed.

explorables.label: Relative positions
explorables.blurb: The authors picked sinusoids because the signal at a shifted position is a linear function of the signal at the original position. They expected this to make relative offsets easy to learn. Learned position embeddings gave nearly identical results.
explorables.quote: We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos+k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos.

explorables.label: 6 + 6 layers
explorables.blurb: The encoder stacks six identical layers, each with self-attention followed by a feed-forward network. The decoder also has six layers and adds a third sub-layer that attends to the encoder's output.
explorables.quote: The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, positionwise fully connected feed-forward network.

explorables.label: Decoder mask
explorables.blurb: In decoder self-attention, links to later positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, which is shown as red cells here. As a result, each prediction can only use the words already produced.
explorables.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

scenes.title: Better translations at a fraction of the cost
scenes.narration: The big model scores 28.4 BLEU on English-to-German and 41.8 on English-to-French after 3.5 days on eight GPUs. The base model trains in 12 hours and still beats earlier ensembles. It also reaches 92.7 F1 on parsing.
scenes.quote: On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, the big transformer model (Transformer (big) in Table 2) outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4.

diagram.title: Better translations at a fraction of the cost
diagram.caption: Table 2 (p. 8): both Transformer sizes match or beat earlier models on WMT 2014 translation while using far fewer training FLOPs. The base model beats every earlier En→De result and trails on En→Fr. Table 4 (p. 10) shows the model also transfers to English constituency parsing.
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the training-budget slider left and watch which models remain affordable, then switch to EN→FR.
diagram.html: The catch: every word attends to every word, so each self-attention layer costs O(n²·d) (Table 1, p. 6).

explorables.label: Training cost (FLOPs)
explorables.blurb: Cost is an estimate, not a measurement. It multiplies training time, the number of GPUs, and each GPU's sustained single-precision throughput, which is 9.5 TFLOPS for a P100.
explorables.quote: We estimate the number of floating point operations used to train a model by multiplying the training time, the number of GPUs used, and an estimate of the sustained single-precision floating-point capacity of each GPU

explorables.label: BLEU on newstest2014
explorables.blurb: BLEU scores translation quality by overlap with reference translations, so higher is better. All translation numbers in the chart come from the WMT 2014 newstest2014 test sets.
explorables.quote: The Transformer achieves better BLEU scores than previous state-of-the-art models on the English-to-German and English-to-French newstest2014 tests at a fraction of the training cost.

explorables.label: Parsing F1 (WSJ 23)
explorables.blurb: A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning reaches 91.3 F1 trained on WSJ alone and 92.7 F1 semi-supervised. Among the models listed, only the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar (93.3) and one multi-task model (93.0) score higher.
explorables.quote: Our results in Table 4 show that despite the lack of task-specific tuning our model performs surprisingly well, yielding better results than all previously reported models with the exception of the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar

scenes.title: Every-word-to-every-word gets costly for long inputs
scenes.narration: All those arcs scale with the square of sentence length, which hurts on very long inputs like images or audio. Output generation is also still one word at a time. The authors leave restricted, local attention for future work.
scenes.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position.

diagram.title: Every-word-to-every-word gets costly for long inputs
diagram.caption: A self-attention layer costs O(n²·d), while attention restricted to a neighborhood of size r would cost O(r·n·d) but stretch the maximum path length to O(n/r) (pp. 6–7). The authors leave local attention, and less sequential generation, for future work (p. 10).
diagram.tryHint: Try: drag the sequence length to the right, then switch restricted attention on and off and watch which arcs from “its” are lost.
diagram.html:
Every-word-to-every-word gets costly for long inputs
Trade-off: max path length O(1) → O(n/r)
Arc weights and sequence lengths are illustrative. Costs O(n²·d) and O(r·n·d) are from Table 1 (p. 6). Restricted attention is proposed, not tested, in the paper.

explorables.label: Quadratic cost
explorables.blurb: Every word scores every other word, so one self-attention layer costs O(n²·d) (Table 1). That is cheap for sentences, where n is usually smaller than d, but it grows fast for long inputs.
explorables.quote: self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d, which is most often the case with sentence representations

explorables.label: Restricted window r
explorables.blurb: The authors suggest a fix in which each position attends only to a neighborhood of r words around it, cutting the cost to O(r·n·d). They propose it but do not test it in the paper.
explorables.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position.

explorables.label: Longer paths trade-off
explorables.blurb: A window costs reach. Distant words, like 'Law' for 'its' in this example, can no longer connect in one step, so the maximum path length grows from O(1) to O(n/r).
explorables.quote: centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r). We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.

explorables.label: One word at a time
explorables.blurb: Training runs in parallel, but the decoder is auto-regressive. It emits one symbol, feeds it back in, then emits the next. The authors name less sequential generation as a research goal.
explorables.quote: Given z, the decoder then generates an output sequence (y1, ..., ym) of symbols one element at a time.

explorables.label: Images, audio, video
explorables.blurb: Non-text inputs such as images, audio and video give much longer sequences than sentences, which is where the n² cost bites. The authors plan to extend the Transformer to them with local, restricted attention.
explorables.quote: We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video.

walkthrough_plan.motif: Our running example is the sentence from the paper's own attention plots: "The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just", drawn as a row of rounded word tiles left to right. Grey tiles are plain words, the tile for "its" is highlighted amber as the query, and violet curved arcs show attention links, with thicker arcs for stronger weights. Slow orange arrows mark sequential RNN steps, green marks parallel computation, and red marks costs or limits.

questions.title: Why can attention link distant words in a single step?
questions.hook: An RNN passes a signal through n steps to connect the first and last word, while self-attention connects every pair at once, trading sequential depth for n² work.
questions.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

questions.title: How does a query pick which values to read?
questions.hook: Attention is a soft dictionary lookup: every key gets a score against the query, and the output blends all values by those scores rather than fetching just one.
questions.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

questions.title: Why divide the dot products by √dₖ?
questions.hook: Without the scale factor, dot-product variance grows with dₖ, so softmax saturates to near one-hot and its gradients almost vanish.
questions.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

questions.title: Why use 8 small heads instead of one big one?
questions.hook: One head has to average everything into a single blend, while eight 64-dim heads at the same total cost can each track a different relation, such as syntax or anaphora.
questions.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

questions.title: How does masking stop the decoder from cheating?
questions.hook: A triangle of −∞ entries in the score matrix, together with shifting the outputs right by one, lets the model train on all positions in parallel without ever seeing the future.
questions.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

questions.title: How do sine waves tell the model word order?
questions.hook: Attention by itself ignores word order, so each position gets a fingerprint of sinusoids at geometrically spaced frequencies; any fixed offset is then a linear function of that fingerprint.
questions.quote: where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid.
